CVE-2021-21974 ESXi OpenSLP Remote code execution in vulnerable OpenSLP service No Historically associated with discussion around the ESXiArgs ransomware.
CVE-2021-22005 vCenter Server Arbitrary file upload leading to remote code execution Yes Documented use in ransomware-related activity.
CVE-2021-21972 vCenter plugin Unauthenticated RCE via vSphere Client plugin Yes Documented use in ransomware-related activity.
CVE-2021-21985 vCenter VSAN Health Check plugin Remote code execution Yes Documented use in ransomware-related activity.
CVE-2023-34048 vCenter DCERPC Out-of-bounds write leading to RCE Yes Known exploited vulnerability affecting vCenter. Although there’s no data about its involvement in ransomware incidents, it is worth noting due to its impact on the virtualization management plane.
CVE-2024-37085 ESXi AD integration AD permissions can become full ESXi administration Yes Documented use in ransomware-related activity. It also highlights the risks arising from the relationship between AD identities and administrative access to ESXi.
CVE-2024-38812 / 38813 vCenter DCERPC RCE / privilege escalation to root Yes Known exploited vulnerabilities affecting vCenter. Although there’s no data about their involvement in ransomware incidents, they are worth noting due to their impact on the virtualization management plane.
CVE-2025-22224 / 22225 / 22226 ESXi / Workstation / Fusion Guest-to-host chain requiring prior guest privileges Yes Known exploited vulnerabilities allowing attackers to perform a guest-to-host attack chain. Where ransomware use is documented, it is stated separately. Neither KEV status nor known exploitation by ransomware actors means that the vulnerability was used in the incident in question.

Active Directory integration

CVE-2024-37085 is a useful illustration of why it is crucial to authenticate to different systems separately even when the hypervisor itself is patched. The vulnerability affects ESXi hosts configured to use AD for user management. According to Microsoft, it is exploited by ransomware operators, including Akira and Black Basta, abusing the ESX Admins group behavior to obtain full ESXi administration. CISA lists the issue in their KEV catalog and notes that it has been used in ransomware incidents.

The vulnerability is fixed in ESXi 8.0 U3. For older systems, Broadcom recommends the following workaround:

  • Change the esxAdminsGroupAutoAdd value from true to false.
  • Change authValidateInterval from 1440 to 90 minutes.
  • Clear the default ESX Admins group mapping where appropriate.

These controls reduce exposure, but the architectural lesson is broader: domain compromise should not automatically allow the adversary to obtain hypervisor admin rights.

Recommendation for defenders

Avoid unnecessary direct Active Directory dependency on ESXi hosts. Where business requirements demand it, stick to the principle of least privilege: add only those accounts to administrative groups that really need this level of access, use separate admin accounts with separate credentials for the domain and for hypervisors, restrict access to the ESXi and vCenter management interfaces to only those network segments, accounts and workstations that are necessary to control it, and continuously validate ESXi permission changes. vCenter role-based access control (RBAC) and identity federation should be configured for virtualization administration, while ordinary enterprise credentials and broad domain groups should not be used to access vCenter or ESXi with high privileges.

Credential reuse from the Windows estate

The third path requires no vulnerability. Administrative credentials present on domain controllers, jump servers, backup systems, identity infrastructure or administrator workstations may provide access to vCenter or ESXi if the same admin accounts are used across different infrastructure segments. MITRE ATT&CK treats the Valid Accounts technique as applicable to ESXi and specifically notes that compromised default or domain accounts can provide privileged access to other systems.

In this incident , credentials obtained from non-virtualization systems inside the organization’s perimeter were used to reach the vCenter Server Appliances. Unlike vulnerability exploitation, successful authentication with a valid account may appear operationally normal. To reliably detect such activity, analysts must therefore evaluate the source host, account history, time, destination, subsequent administrative actions, and whether the authenticated account normally manages virtualization infrastructure.

Backup infrastructure as a credential bridge

Backup platforms are not passive storage. They commonly require service accounts, hypervisor credentials, repository access and broad network reach so they can protect and restore critical workloads. This makes the backup server a concentrated trust point. In this incident, the adversary extracted stored credentials after gaining administrative execution on backup infrastructure, creating a route toward other infrastructure tiers.

Persistence on the management plane

With the potential risk possibilities explained, let’s go back to our case study. The attackers managed to compromise via SSH the vCenter appliance managing virtualization disaster recovery where they established two layers of persistence. The first used MeshAgent, the endpoint component of the legitimate MeshCentral remote management platform. The second used Ligolo-ng as a reverse tunnel implemented as a systemd service. This activity maps to two ATT&CK techniques: Systemd Service (T1543.002) and Protocol Tunneling (T1572).

The timeline was as follows. The attackers authenticated on the appliance as root via SSH. Forty-three seconds later, they fetched and deployed MeshAgent through a shell script. The SSH session lasted 2 minutes and 26 seconds in total. After it ended, the adversary didn’t use SSH to access the compromised appliance anymore, thus reducing the usefulness of monitoring focused only on interactive SSH sessions. Roughly four hours later, they returned through MeshAgent and installed the Ligolo-ng tunnel as a persistent systemd unit.

Unit file    /etc/systemd/system/vmware-vdma.service
Service      vmware-vdma
Description  "DNS, time, VM settings sync (v2.03.24766)"
ExecStart    /opt/vmware/bin/agent
Restart      always

The unit uses a VMware-like prefix, places its binary under /opt/vmware/bin/, describes plausible appliance housekeeping functions, and requests Restart=always. A defender should not treat any unrecognized VMware-looking service as malicious by default, because custom integrations may exist, but a service absent from the list of services the organization defines as trusted is a high-confidence anomaly requiring immediate validation.

Beyond the incident in question, more advanced ESXi persistence techniques have also been documented. For example, Mandiant observed attackers using malicious vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) as a persistence mechanism on compromised ESXi hosts. This demonstrates that attackers with administrative access can establish persistent access at the hypervisor layer, including persistence that survives host restarts. However, this incident shows that common remote-management software and a systemd service can be sufficient when vCenter itself is trusted and poorly monitored.

Turning vCenter into an offensive control plane

One interesting technique observed in the incident was the use of vCenter Host Profiles. Host Profiles are intended to capture and enforce configuration across ESXi hosts. A Host Profile can be applied to separate hosts, clusters of hosts or all hosts associated with a profile. It also may contain subprofiles covering specific configuration aspects, e.g., authentication. Among other things, Host Profiles may contain configuration for Tech Support Mode (TSM) and TSM-SSH.

In this incident, the adversary used Host Profiles to change TSM-SSH service state to enable SSH on target ESXi hosts. The evidence recorded the following sequence:

Offset Source Observed event Primary evidence
T+0 vCenter Host configuration read through Host Profile workflow vpxa.log
T+10m18s vCenter Configuration change pushed to enable SSH vpxa.log
T+10m51s vCenter / ESXi TSM-SSH service reached RUNNING state, indicating that SSH has been enabled on the host and it is accessible from a remote device vpxa.log + vobd.log

Host Profile manipulation sequence observed before direct ESXi access

Note that the 33-second interval between the configuration push and TSM-SSH reaching RUNNING state is short enough for us to be able to quickly correlate these events by comparing logs from different sources. Overall, it took the attacker eleven minutes after the initial configuration read to reconfigure the host from policy-disabled SSH to direct remote access support. Subsequently, direct SSH access to the target ESXi hosts originated from the vCenter appliance IP, a source that would normally be considered highly trusted on the management network.

Compromise of the management plane converted a legitimate compliance mechanism into an access path to the managed hypervisor

Why ESXi configuration change via vCenter is a trust-boundary failure

Host hardening is important, but centrally administered controls should not be considered independent once the central management tool is compromised. If vCenter has authority to modify host state, an attacker controlling it may be able to make a malicious change look structurally similar to legitimate compliance activity: read configuration, apply a desired state, and observe the result. The distinguishing context becomes authorization, the timing, the source account, the change window, and whether the desired state itself weakens security.

This is why vCenter should be treated as a Tier 0 asset and provided with the highest possible level of protection. Management-plane administrative accounts should be isolated from ordinary enterprise administration, network access should be restricted to dedicated management paths, high-risk configuration changes should require strong authentication and monitoring, and vCenter-to-ESXi traffic should be thoroughly compared to a normal behavior baseline (connection patterns, ports, protocols, source and destination systems) rather than implicitly trusted. All significant discrepancies should be treated as suspicious and investigated.

High-fidelity detection opportunity

An alert should be generated when Host Profile compliance (or remediation in VMware terms) changes TSM or TSM-SSH configuration outside an approved window, particularly when followed by a new SSH session from vCenter or another management appliance. This sequence is more precise than alerting on SSH alone because each step is legitimate in isolation but dangerous in combination.

Notes on ESXi abuse: living-off-the-land tools and controls to monitor

Once an attacker can administer ESXi, many destructive actions require no exploit. LOLESXi project catalogs native ESXi binaries and scripts that have been abused by threat actors, including administrative utilities that enumerate VMs, control power state and alter configuration. This mirrors living-off-the-land behavior on Windows, but the target is the hypervisor control plane.

There are two ESXi hardening mechanisms, and changes to either can be viewed as highly suspicious. Host acceptance level controls which VIBs are allowed to install. The execInstalledOnly setting controls whether non-installed binaries may execute. Broadcom states that ESXi 8 enables the execInstalledOnly runtime option by default and warns that disabling it allows unknown non-installed binaries to execute, increasing ransomware risk. There is also a kernel enforcement setting with the same name, which is related to the runtime option, but distinct. Changes to that may require a reboot.

execInstalledOnly runtime Execution of binaries not installed through VIB packages Value 0/FALSE permits non-installed code to run vobd.log + advanced settings

Ransomware family Observed or documented VM stop approach
GwisinLocker, LockBit, Conti Enumerate worlds with a esxcli vm process list command and terminate individual worlds with a esxcli vm process kill command.

Authors

  • Oleg Kupreev

In August 2026, we detected a new variant of the CoffeeLoader malware in the wild. On launch, the NSIS-based installer executable dropped a file named 7z.dll into a temporary directory and ran it through rundll32.exe. The 7z.dll file was a patched version of the original library of the popular 7-Zip archiver. Part of its code had been replaced with malicious self-decrypting shellcode that turned out to be a new version of the Armoury packer. This packer was also previously used in the CoffeeLoader Trojan.

New Armoury variant

The old variant of the Armoury packer used the GPU to decrypt the Trojan’s main body, relying on the OpenCL library, which implements the standard of the same name for high-performance computing.

}

The new variant also utilizes the GPU, but instead of OpenCL, it uses the OpenGL library, which implements the eponymous standard for applications that work with 2D and 3D graphics.

The first shellcode is a dropper responsible for installing the Trojan and gaining persistence. To do this, it copies the library to Windows folders and adds it to autorun. The second is a stager that creates a new dllhost.exe process and injects the main body of CoffeeLoader into it; in this variant, the main body is an executable file. Unlike the old version, the new version of the packer delivers yet another shellcode.

CoffeeLoader downloader

The shellcode decrypted by the Armoury packer is a new intermediate link in the infection chain: the CoffeeLoader downloader. It fully incorporates the dropper and stager functionality described above, as well as downloader functions used to fetch the Trojan’s main body.

New CoffeeLoader downloader viewed in a text editor

To establish persistence, the Trojan copies 7z.dll to subfolders of %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%. The Run registry key is used for autorun. The subfolder, library, and registry value are named with eight hexadecimal digits generated from system volume information.

item.title: Operation ShadowCloud: cloud service–based backdoors targeting government networks in Asia and Africa. Part 1
item.description:
Authors

  • Saurabh Sharma
  • Noushin Shabab

Introduction

In early 2026, we identified a new, active intrusion campaign that we have named Operation ShadowCloud. The threat actor behind it is abusing the legitimate MeshAgent utility to drop two brand-new backdoors. GraphDoor (MD5 14ec33ea808e697870d00c5e434c2952)

The malware begins by opening a named pipe that it will reuse for later communications, building the pipe’s name from its own PID in the form \\.\pipe\p%lu (where %lu is the process ID as an unsigned long integer). Once the backdoor contacts its C2 server and downloads the required plug-ins, those plug-ins write their status reports to the same pipe.

After the pipe is set up, the backdoor creates a directory named Intel_Log inside the system’s ProgramData folder. Inside that folder, it generates a subdirectory whose name is a randomly generated GUID, yielding a full path like C:\ProgramData\Intel_Log\<random‑GUID>.

Next, the malware starts gathering system information to send back to the attacker. It resolves the needed Windows APIs at runtime by hashing DLL and function names with the DJB2 algorithm. To invoke these APIs covertly, the backdoor installs a vectored exception handler that contains a miniature routine for the desired call, then deliberately raises an exception. The handler catches the exception, runs the routine, and thus calls the target API. Using this indirect call technique, the malware harvests the following information from the victim machine:

  • Network adapter details
  • Version of the operating system
  • A randomly generated GUID for the infected machine
  • Public IP
  • Private IP
  • Username
  • Host name
  • Current directory (where the backdoor is executed from)
  • PID of its own module
  • A list of all the running processes

In addition to the victim information, the backdoor also decrypts a set of embedded configuration parameters (see the list below) and appends them to the victim data. The resulting information is then encrypted with AES, Base64‑encoded, and transmitted to the command‑and‑control server.

  • "type":"serv"
  • "client_version":"1.2.7"
  • "dhj_exe":"javaw.exe"
  • "execution_method":"normal"
  • "is_need_lock":"false"

  • UUID path segment
  • Client ID (application registration)
  • Client secret

It also generates a random X‑CSRF‑TOKEN, decrypts a preset User‑Agent string and several other hard-coded strings, and then issues a POST request to login.microsoftonline.com (see the example below). item.title: The forced audit: how AuditTeam’s OpsAgent framework masks ransomware as consulting
item.description:
Authors

  • Vladimir Nestor

AuditTeam is an active threat group that uses the OpsAgent framework to compromise organizations across at least seven countries and territories. The campaign began in January 2026 and remained active through October 2026, at a minimum. In its ransom note, AuditTeam demands an “Audit & Consulting fee” in exchange for vulnerability reports. During this period, the group has infected dozens of organizations in Russia, Italy, the Philippines, Hong Kong, Senegal, Finland and China. The group’s leak site also claims victims in seven additional countries.

OpsAgent provides file system management, process injection, privilege escalation, keylogging, screenshot capture, and network pivoting. During the campaign OpsAgent was transitioned from C++ to Rust while adding new capabilities including interactive shells and WebSocket upgrades. Its command-and-control domains use Amazon CloudFront subdomains, which OpsAgent discovers via a public GitHub repository. Two specialized modules extend its functionality. An antivirus/endpoint detection and response (AV/EDR) killer module installs a digitally signed Beijing Jiangmin Antivirus driver to terminate security products. A cryptor module encrypts files using AES-CBC or ChaCha20 with X25519 key exchange and targets database processes for termination prior to doing so.

Background

On March 10, 2026, we discovered suspicious activity targeting an organization in Hong Kong. The tool used was OpsAgent, a framework designed to resemble a penetration testing utility. Further investigation revealed attacks in additional countries, prompting an active research phase. This implant offers extensive operator capabilities, including host reconnaissance, shellcode injection via named pipes, and lateral movement through agent networks based on compromised hosts.

Analysis indicates OpsAgent was used by AuditTeam. The group was first mentioned publicly by dbdigest.com in March 2026. On June 25, 2026, DeXpose reported that AuditTeam had claimed responsibility for an attack on a Russian organization and listed it on its leak site. AuditTeam leaves a ransom note threatening to release stolen data unless a fee is paid. They call this fee the “Audit & Consulting fee.” According to the note, payment results in a vulnerability report being delivered to the victim instead of leaking the stolen data archive to the public internet. While the note does not mention file encryption, it is left by the cryptor module. Therefore, if a victim sees the note, their files are already encrypted.

The ransom note

GitHub commit history shows the campaign started on January 5, 2026. The leak site lists its first victim on February 21, 2026. Dozens of machines across at least seven countries were infected. On August 19, 2026, a C2 domain for the new OpsAgent version was added to the public repository and subsequently used in attacks.

AuditTeam activity timeline

Technical details

Loaders

OpsAgent uses multiple loader variants during its campaign. All discovered loaders unpack OpsAgent by parsing the MZ header and transferring execution to the entry point of the unpacked payload.

The C loader was discovered in April 2026. It injects shellcode into msiexec.exe using standard API calls: CreateProcessA, VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateRemoteThread.

The .NET loader was found in June 2026. It uses NtQueueApcThread instead of direct process creation for injection. It contains strings such as DApc, DProtect, DResume, and msiexec.exe. Both the C and .NET loaders inject shellcode into a separate target process. They are also protected by OLLVM obfuscation with control-flow flattening enabled.

In September 2026, we discovered the Rust loader. It retrieves an encrypted payload from the C2 server, decrypts it, parses the PE header, and runs the Execute export function within its own process rather than injecting into another process. This in-process execution model eliminates the need for remote process manipulation.

OpsAgent main implant

The implant (version 5.2.8) rivals Cobalt Strike in functionality. It uses a worker-thread architecture: the main thread monitors connection health, while a worker thread processes commands from a queue. Three concepts structure its behavior:

  • the worker thread (handles nearly all C2 commands)
  • jobs (background tasks run in separate processes)
  • links (connections to child agents used for lateral movement)

Exceptions include info, jobs, jobkill, worker_status, worker_restart, and exit, which execute immediately in the main thread.

OpsAgent can optionally obtain its C2 address by reading a public GitHub repository: hxxps://github[.]com/RonaldCMalcolm1983/staticPage. The address is stored in an encrypted form using AES‑CBC with the SHA‑256 hash of f4bb8c7e15d8b98d535eb20b09176b3d as the key and a zero initialization vector. The encrypted payload is wrapped with the markers GetConfig and EndConfig and then base64‑encoded.

Several commands — mimikatz_spawn, execute_assembly, pth_spawn, runpe, monitor start, and screenshot_service start — run background jobs in a separate process. To run a job, each creates a process and a named pipe, and receives shellcode from the C2 server. No command contains embedded mimikatz or PTH binaries. All payloads arrive remotely through the pipe, encrypted with XOR using key 604902af7b70b271. By default these commands use msiexec.exe as a host process, but the path can be changed. The exception is the monitor command, which uses notepad.exe for shellcode injection. This design keeps the implant small and lets operators deliver custom payloads remotely.

Injection commands support two modes: Legacy and DbgInjector. Legacy mode uses CreateProcessA and NtCreateThreadEx. DbgInjector creates a process in DEBUG state, allocates shared memory, sets a hardware breakpoint on FileTimeToSystemTime, then redirects RIP to the shellcode without creating a new thread.

Several code patterns suggest LLM-assisted development. For example, OpsAgent resolves WinAPI functions dynamically by hash: it calculates the hash of a function name, then searches for the matching address. Sometimes the plaintext name remains in memory before hashing. Additionally, all injection commands share near‑identical code structures, differing only in argument count and target process selection. This uniform approach matches LLM‑generated scaffolding.

Commands description

The OpsAgent command set covers file system operations, process management, privilege escalation, shellcode injection, monitoring, and network pivoting. The C2 protocol runs over WebSocket with TLS and exchanges data in units called frames. Protocol frame types function as an extra command set enabling SOCKS proxy establishment, chunked file uploads, and inter-agent data forwarding. These frames are handled by a dedicated frame-handler function rather than the standard command decoder. The following combined table lists all text-based commands and protocol frame types together.

Several commands deserve closer attention. The monitor command manages keylogging through subcommands that start, stop, and configure logging threads. Screenshot features follow a similar design with session management subcommands. In contrast, the pivot subsystem uses a flatter command structure where each pivot command (pivot_list, pivot_start, pivot_stop, pivot_add, pivot_remove, pivot_auto) operates independently without nested subcommand hierarchies.

Some frame type numbers such as 0x20 appear unused in the current implementation. These may be traces of previous versions.

Additional modules

AV/EDR killer module

This module installs a driver disguised as Beijing Jiangmin Antivirus (KV series), utilizing the \KvCorePortX0 filter port for communication. Upon receiving the 0x1D command followed by a target filename, the driver terminates the corresponding process. Its target list covers nearly every major security product on the market.

Additionally, the driver carries a valid digital signature, which facilitates its initial execution.

The process kill list contains approximately 220 entries, including:

    • Security products: MsMpEng, SecurityHealthService, avp, ekrn, ccSvcHst, fcag, eadrline
    • Remote access tools: TeamViewer_Desktop, TeamViewer_Service, tv_w32, tv_x64
    • Monitoring/logging: Sysmon, Sysmon64, splunkd, wazuh-agent
    • Backup services: VeeamNFSSvc, AcronisAgent, MBAMService
    • Database processes: sqlservr, mysqld, mongod, redis-server

Cryptor module

This module encrypts files using either AES-CBC or ChaCha20 based on a command-line flag. Each file receives a unique encryption key produced by RtlGenRandom. A 12-byte array serves as the ChaCha20 nonce or expands to a 16-byte AES initialization vector. Key exchange relies on X25519 Diffie-Hellman with a static public key embedded in the binary. The module generates an ephemeral key pair per session and encrypts the file key with ChaCha20 using the shared secret.

Beyond file encryption, the module actively disrupts infrastructure by terminating database processes including SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis. It also stops backup services such as Veeam. The module removes shadow copies, empties the recycle bin, and wipes temporary folders. Furthermore, any file deletion overwrites content with random data before removing the entry, preventing forensic recovery.

After encryption, the module drops a ransom note. It formats the message as an audit log demanding payment through a Tor onion address. The note offers two options: pay the “Audit & Consulting fee” for a vulnerability report or face public data disclosure.

Finally, the module’s configuration parameters include file extensions to encrypt, directories and files to whitelist, processes and services to terminate, and shadow copy deletion flags.

OpsAgent-rs (Rust version)

The Rust rewrite maintains functional parity with the C++ version while introducing new capabilities. OpsAgent-rs initially communicates with the C2 via HTTP POST requests to retrieve commands. There are special commands that change this behavior. After receiving an upgrade command, the implant establishes a persistent WebSocket connection over TLS for ongoing C2 communication instead of continuing to send POST requests. Additionally, command identifiers shifted from text names to numeric constants. New commands include interactive shells, directory creation, and sleep-interval changes.

Command mapping between versions shows most legacy commands have Rust equivalents. However, screenshot and monitor commands now consolidate into a unified identifier rather than relying on an extensive set of subcommands. The Rust version removes the entire pivot command set, eliminating pivoting task management functionality.

C2 acquisition in the Rust version changed significantly. The configuration contains a flag controlling whether the implant checks GitHub for new C2 addresses. It also stores markers indicating the beginning and end of the encrypted C2 string. The GitHub README page holds both the legacy C2 format and an additional base64-encoded blob specifically for OpsAgent-rs. The encryption scheme was reworked to use AES-GCM instead of AES-CBC. To derive the GCM key, the decryption flow computes HMAC-SHA256 of the secret key c2-framework-psk-salt-v1 against the configuration data blob, then applies a second HMAC with the salt c2-encryption-key\x01. The nonce is the first 12 bytes of the decrypted payload and the tag occupies the last 16 bytes.

Infrastructure

The implant uses AWS-generated CloudFront CDN subdomains as C2 endpoints. Because these domains operate on shared infrastructure, their underlying IP addresses cannot serve as reliable standalone IOCs.

– 157.20.104.111 Aug 19, 2026 Aug 24, 2026 AS 136557

The GitHub repository stayed active throughout the campaign until November 2026. Commit history shows ongoing updates until September 29, 2026, when the actor deleted the legacy C2 domain from the repository. This suggests the actor maintains the infrastructure actively and rotates domains as needed.

In November 2026, the GitHub repository was removed. However, this does not mean the campaign is over, as the latest Rust implants found contained a configuration with the GitHub feature disabled.

Victims

AuditTeam targets organizations from different countries and territories. We observed victims in China, the Philippines, Senegal, Italy, Finland, Hong Kong and Russia. And according to the group’s leak site, there are victims in Turkey, Thailand, Ukraine, Argentina, South Korea, Japan, and Spain. All identified victims belong to different industries.

Attribution

We attribute the OpsAgent campaign to AuditTeam with high confidence. The following evidence supports this assessment:

  • Ransom note format and “Audit & Consulting fee” terminology unique to this group
  • Tor-based leak site listing targeted organizations
  • Operational philosophy distinguishing them from conventional ransomware groups through remediation reports

Open sources first identified AuditTeam in March 2026 via dbdigest.com. In June, DeXpose reported that AuditTeam claimed responsibility for attacking a Russian organization and listed it on its leak site. The group claims a mission to educate organizations about cybersecurity through exploitation and remediation reports. This tactical approach separates them from traditional ransomware operators.

Conclusions

AuditTeam frames extortion as a paid security audit — a distinctive model among ransomware groups. The C++ to Rust transition signals continued toolchain investment. New Rust commands cover interactive shells, WebSocket upgrades, and directory management.

The specialized modules reveal thorough operational preparation: the AV/EDR killer uses a signed Jiangmin driver to disable security products, and the cryptor module terminates database processes, encrypts files, and removes shadow copies. These tools let the group neutralize defenses and optionally destroy data.

CloudFront CDN subdomains complicate takedown and make IP-based blocking impractical because the IP space is shared with legitimate traffic. While the actor rotates infrastructure, the public GitHub repository enables C2 discovery and its removal disrupts the attack chain.

Custom malware frameworks are typically developed and maintained by APT groups with dedicated engineering resources. AuditTeam shows that a ransomware crew can build comparable tooling. This shift may be enabled by AI-assisted development tools lowering the barrier to creating functional, multi-module implant architectures.

In September 2026, we discovered the Rust loader. It retrieves an encrypted payload from the C2 server, decrypts it, parses the PE header, and runs the Execute export function within its own process rather than injecting into another process. This in-process execution model eliminates the need for remote process manipulation.

OpsAgent main implant

The implant (version 5.2.8) rivals Cobalt Strike in functionality. It uses a worker-thread architecture: the main thread monitors connection health, while a worker thread processes commands from a queue. Three concepts structure its behavior:

  • the worker thread (handles nearly all C2 commands)
  • jobs (background tasks run in separate processes)
  • links (connections to child agents used for lateral movement)

Exceptions include info, jobs, jobkill, worker_status, worker_restart, and exit, which execute immediately in the main thread.

OpsAgent can optionally obtain its C2 address by reading a public GitHub repository: hxxps://github[.]com/RonaldCMalcolm1983/staticPage. The address is stored in an encrypted form using AES‑CBC with the SHA‑256 hash of f4bb8c7e15d8b98d535eb20b09176b3d as the key and a zero initialization vector. The encrypted payload is wrapped with the markers GetConfig and EndConfig and then base64‑encoded.

Several commands — mimikatz_spawn, execute_assembly, pth_spawn, runpe, monitor start, and screenshot_service start — run background jobs in a separate process. To run a job, each creates a process and a named pipe, and receives shellcode from the C2 server. No command contains embedded mimikatz or PTH binaries. All payloads arrive remotely through the pipe, encrypted with XOR using key 604902af7b70b271. By default these commands use msiexec.exe as a host process, but the path can be changed. The exception is the monitor command, which uses notepad.exe for shellcode injection. This design keeps the implant small and lets operators deliver custom payloads remotely.

Injection commands support two modes: Legacy and DbgInjector. Legacy mode uses CreateProcessA and NtCreateThreadEx. DbgInjector creates a process in DEBUG state, allocates shared memory, sets a hardware breakpoint on FileTimeToSystemTime, then redirects RIP to the shellcode without creating a new thread.

Several code patterns suggest LLM-assisted development. For example, OpsAgent resolves WinAPI functions dynamically by hash: it calculates the hash of a function name, then searches for the matching address. Sometimes the plaintext name remains in memory before hashing. Additionally, all injection commands share near‑identical code structures, differing only in argument count and target process selection. This uniform approach matches LLM‑generated scaffolding.

Commands description

The OpsAgent command set covers file system operations, process management, privilege escalation, shellcode injection, monitoring, and network pivoting. The C2 protocol runs over WebSocket with TLS and exchanges data in units called frames. Protocol frame types function as an extra command set enabling SOCKS proxy establishment, chunked file uploads, and inter-agent data forwarding. These frames are handled by a dedicated frame-handler function rather than the standard command decoder. The following combined table lists all text-based commands and protocol frame types together.

Several commands deserve closer attention. The monitor command manages keylogging through subcommands that start, stop, and configure logging threads. Screenshot features follow a similar design with session management subcommands. In contrast, the pivot subsystem uses a flatter command structure where each pivot command (pivot_list, pivot_start, pivot_stop, pivot_add, pivot_remove, pivot_auto) operates independently without nested subcommand hierarchies.

Some frame type numbers such as 0x20 appear unused in the current implementation. These may be traces of previous versions.

Additional modules

AV/EDR killer module

This module installs a driver disguised as Beijing Jiangmin Antivirus (KV series), utilizing the \KvCorePortX0 filter port for communication. Upon receiving the 0x1D command followed by a target filename, the driver terminates the corresponding process. Its target list covers nearly every major security product on the market.

Additionally, the driver carries a valid digital signature, which facilitates its initial execution.

The process kill list contains approximately 220 entries, including:

    • Security products: MsMpEng, SecurityHealthService, avp, ekrn, ccSvcHst, fcag, eadrline
    • Remote access tools: TeamViewer_Desktop, TeamViewer_Service, tv_w32, tv_x64
    • Monitoring/logging: Sysmon, Sysmon64, splunkd, wazuh-agent
    • Backup services: VeeamNFSSvc, AcronisAgent, MBAMService
    • Database processes: sqlservr, mysqld, mongod, redis-server

Cryptor module

This module encrypts files using either AES-CBC or ChaCha20 based on a command-line flag. Each file receives a unique encryption key produced by RtlGenRandom. A 12-byte array serves as the ChaCha20 nonce or expands to a 16-byte AES initialization vector. Key exchange relies on X25519 Diffie-Hellman with a static public key embedded in the binary. The module generates an ephemeral key pair per session and encrypts the file key with ChaCha20 using the shared secret.

Beyond file encryption, the module actively disrupts infrastructure by terminating database processes including SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis. It also stops backup services such as Veeam. The module removes shadow copies, empties the recycle bin, and wipes temporary folders. Furthermore, any file deletion overwrites content with random data before removing the entry, preventing forensic recovery.

After encryption, the module drops a ransom note. It formats the message as an audit log demanding payment through a Tor onion address. The note offers two options: pay the “Audit & Consulting fee” for a vulnerability report or face public data disclosure.

Finally, the module’s configuration parameters include file extensions to encrypt, directories and files to whitelist, processes and services to terminate, and shadow copy deletion flags.

OpsAgent-rs (Rust version)

The Rust rewrite maintains functional parity with the C++ version while introducing new capabilities. OpsAgent-rs initially communicates with the C2 via HTTP POST requests to retrieve commands. There are special commands that change this behavior. After receiving an upgrade command, the implant establishes a persistent WebSocket connection over TLS for ongoing C2 communication instead of continuing to send POST requests. Additionally, command identifiers shifted from text names to numeric constants. New commands include interactive shells, directory creation, and sleep-interval changes.

Command mapping between versions shows most legacy commands have Rust equivalents. However, screenshot and monitor commands now consolidate into a unified identifier rather than relying on an extensive set of subcommands. The Rust version removes the entire pivot command set, eliminating pivoting task management functionality.

C2 acquisition in the Rust version changed significantly. The configuration contains a flag controlling whether the implant checks GitHub for new C2 addresses. It also stores markers indicating the beginning and end of the encrypted C2 string. The GitHub README page holds both the legacy C2 format and an additional base64-encoded blob specifically for OpsAgent-rs. The encryption scheme was reworked to use AES-GCM instead of AES-CBC. To derive the GCM key, the decryption flow computes HMAC-SHA256 of the secret key c2-framework-psk-salt-v1 against the configuration data blob, then applies a second HMAC with the salt c2-encryption-key\x01. The nonce is the first 12 bytes of the decrypted payload and the tag occupies the last 16 bytes.

Infrastructure

The implant uses AWS-generated CloudFront CDN subdomains as C2 endpoints. Because these domains operate on shared infrastructure, their underlying IP addresses cannot serve as reliable standalone IOCs.

The GitHub repository stayed active throughout the campaign until November 2026. Commit history shows ongoing updates until September 29, 2026, when the actor deleted the legacy C2 domain from the repository. This suggests the actor maintains the infrastructure actively and rotates domains as needed.

In November 2026, the GitHub repository was removed. However, this does not mean the campaign is over, as the latest Rust implants found contained a configuration with the GitHub feature disabled.

Victims

AuditTeam targets organizations from different countries and territories. We observed victims in China, the Philippines, Senegal, Italy, Finland, Hong Kong and Russia. And according to the group’s leak site, there are victims in Turkey, Thailand, Ukraine, Argentina, South Korea, Japan, and Spain. All identified victims belong to different industries.

Attribution

We attribute the OpsAgent campaign to AuditTeam with high confidence. The following evidence supports this assessment:

  • Ransom note format and “Audit & Consulting fee” terminology unique to this group
  • Tor-based leak site listing targeted organizations
  • Operational philosophy distinguishing them from conventional ransomware groups through remediation reports

Open sources first identified AuditTeam in March 2026 via dbdigest.com. In June, DeXpose reported that AuditTeam claimed responsibility for attacking a Russian organization and listed it on its leak site. The group claims a mission to educate organizations about cybersecurity through exploitation and remediation reports. This tactical approach separates them from traditional ransomware operators.

Conclusions

AuditTeam frames extortion as a paid security audit — a distinctive model among ransomware groups. The C++ to Rust transition signals continued toolchain investment. New Rust commands cover interactive shells, WebSocket upgrades, and directory management.

The specialized modules reveal thorough operational preparation: the AV/EDR killer uses a signed Jiangmin driver to disable security products, and the cryptor module terminates database processes, encrypts files, and removes shadow copies. These tools let the group neutralize defenses and optionally destroy data.

CloudFront CDN subdomains complicate takedown and make IP-based blocking impractical because the IP space is shared with legitimate traffic. While the actor rotates infrastructure, the public GitHub repository enables C2 discovery and its removal disrupts the attack chain.

Custom malware frameworks are typically developed and maintained by APT groups with dedicated engineering resources. AuditTeam shows that a ransomware crew can build comparable tooling. item.title: Black Friday, red flags: too-good-to-be-true deals hiding real threats (2026)
item.description:
Authors

  • Kaspersky

Intro

Black Friday remains a defining moment of the holiday shopping season and a key period for cybercriminals seeking to exploit the surge in consumer activity. The scale of this demand is reflected in seasonal spending patterns. According to PwC’s post-holiday analysis, holiday spending rose by 6.4% year over year in 2025, with Black Friday once again being the peak sales day generating nearly $20 billion. Consumer behavior points to the same trend: KPMG’s 2026 Consumer Pulse Survey found that Black Friday remains the most important sales event, with 62% of respondents pointing to its importance. Moreover, it is strongly associated with online shopping, with 83% of consumers preferring to buy online or combine online and in-person purchases on this occasion. To find the best offers, 55% of respondents in 2026 planned to research purchases through retailer websites and 46% through brand websites. As shopping activity concentrates online during peak sales periods, threat actors gain broader opportunities to exploit consumer demand, trusted brands, and heavy promotional traffic to steal credentials, payment data, and money.

At Kaspersky, we closely follow the cybersecurity risks associated with major shopping events and seasonal spikes in online retail activity. Our annual analysis examines how cybercriminals adapt their tactics to target consumers during high-demand sales periods.

This report extends our annual Securelist series published in 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025, exploring how shopping-related cyberthreats continue to evolve.

Methodology

To keep pace with the evolving shopping threat landscape, we conduct an annual assessment of the most prevalent malicious techniques, including financial malware, phishing pages impersonating major retailers, e-commerce platforms, digital services, banks, and payment providers, as well as spam campaigns designed to steer users to fraudulent sites. The threat data we rely on is sourced from Kaspersky Security Network (KSN), which processes anonymized cybersecurity data shared consensually by Kaspersky users.

Most of the data in this report draws on was collected from January through October 2026.

Key findings

  • In the first ten months of 2026, Kaspersky identified more than 19 million phishing attacks targeting users of online stores, payment systems and banks, a year-on-year increase of 1%.
  • As many as 5% of these attacks were directed at online shoppers.
  • Around 84% of all phishing attacks targeting users of online stores and subscription services involve scammers impersonating Amazon, Apple, Netflix, Shopify and Alibaba Group pages.
  • Netflix-themed phishing detections grew by 5% in 2026 in comparison with 2025 data.
  • We detected more than 220,071 sales-themed spam messages in the first two weeks of November, which is 50.2% more than in 2025.
  • More than 801,000 banking Trojan attacks were recorded during the first 10 months of 2026.
  • Between June and November 2026, Kaspersky products have already detected over 27,000 attacks by malware and potentially unwanted applications posing as GTA VI-related content.

Shopping-related phishing by the numbers

Phishing and scams remain among the most persistent threats for online shoppers, particularly during peak sales periods, when heightened transaction volumes and time-sensitive offers create conditions for abuse. One of the most notable developments in recent years has been the growing use of AI to increase the speed, scale and sophistication of such campaigns. AI-enabled tools can be used to generate convincing phishing emails, fraudulent shopping pages, and realistic seller identities, while also adapting messages and visuals to mimic legitimate brands. In the context of major retail events, where consumers often move quickly across marketplaces, social platforms, and promotional channels, this added level of automation further increases the risk of deception, credential theft, and financial loss.

Although phishing has long remained a common method of deceiving users, we are seeing a growing number of attacks in segments related to online shopping. From January through October 2026, Kaspersky products blocked 19,063,077 attempts to access phishing links targeting users of online stores, payment systems, and banks – nearly three times (198.1%) more than during the same period last year, when 6,394,854 such attempts were recorded. A breakdown of these attempts shows that 44.54% targeted online shoppers, compared with 48.21% in 2025; 28.55% targeted banking users, up from 26.10%; and 26.91% mimicked payment systems, versus 25.69% last year.

Financial phishing attacks by category, January–October 2026 (download)

Since 2021, we have conducted annual assessments of the distribution of phishing attacks targeting users across popular online platforms, including Amazon, Alibaba Group, eBay, Mercado Libre, and Walmart, in order to track how the attackers abuse trusted brands. In 2026, Kaspersky products detected and blocked 3,102,304 phishing attempts involving the misuse of Amazon’s brand, up 411.6% from 606,369 attempts in 2025. Threat actors consistently stick to leveraging well-known and trusted consumer platforms to enhance the credibility of fraudulent pages.

Other major e-commerce brands were also widely impersonated in phishing campaigns. Kaspersky detected 360,949 attempts to visit phishing pages mimicking Alibaba-owned brands including AliExpress, while eBay-themed phishing pages accounted for 163,381 alerts. The Latin American marketplace Mercado Libre was used as a lure in 109,081 cases, and Walmart-related phishing pages were identified 74,220 times.

Popular online stores mimicked by scammers, January–October 2026 (download)

The rankings of platforms most frequently impersonated by scammers include more than just brands directly associated with tangible items. The attackers are equally interested in scamming users of popular services selling digital products, such as music, TV shows, e-books, and others. The overall top five brands abused in 2026 were Amazon, Apple, Netflix, Shopify, and Alibaba Group–associated brands, which together were mimicked in 7,119,400 detections. Overall, these five platforms represented 83.83% of all phishing attacks associated with online stores and subscription services.

TOP 5 online platforms mimicked by scammers, January–October 2026 (download)

As mentioned before, Amazon was abused in 3,102,304 detections, or 36.53% of the total. Phishing pages impersonating Apple-related resources accounted for 1,622,917 detections, or 19.1%. Netflix-themed phishing accounted for 1,365,648 detections, or 16.08% of the total, marking a 70.5% increase from 801,148 detections recorded in 2025. Shopify-themed phishing accounted for 667,582 detections, or 7.86%.

What mass scam campaigns look like

Mass scam campaigns often rely on phishing kits or templates that can be used to quickly build numerous pages that target different markets, languages, and user segments and mimic widely used platforms. These platforms are broadly recognized and generally trusted by the users, while standardized scam flows allow attackers to scale operations with minimal effort. Across these campaigns, scammers combine familiar visual design, urgent calls to action, and fake login, payment, or verification pages.

Brand recognition in this scenario works against users: the more familiar an interface looks, the less likely a visitor is to question its authenticity. This logic forms the basis of a whole cluster of phishing campaigns that abuse the names of major tech platforms. Fraudulent pages copying login pages of these platforms reproduce the original layout, branding, and even alternative sign-in options, leaving credential entry forms as the only interactive element – everything typed into these forms goes straight to the attackers. Hijacked logins to an e-commerce platform potentially open the door not only to the victims’ purchase history or payment methods in this exact store, but also to other accounts that use the same login credentials.

Scammers often create pages that replicate the fonts and visual style of the original site. This example mimics an Amazon page

A common technique for stealing login credentials. Example of a fake website impersonating Shopify

A related but noisier approach relies on manufactured urgency: we detected pages masquerading as Apple support that bombard the visitor with alarming pop-ups about a suspicious Apple Pay “pre-authorization” and urge them to immediately call a “support number”. If the user contacts the phone number, fake operators will try to talk the victim into revealing sensitive details or granting remote access to their device, which can be used to steal money and data. Despite differing mechanics, both approaches exploit the same vulnerability – reflexive trust in a familiar brand whose identity the scammers have appropriated – and simply choose different triggers: routine in the first case, panic in the second.

Example of a scam page exploiting a sense of urgency

There’s usually a variety of scams abusing users’ trust and the hype surrounding Apple devices. Fake stores appearing to sell or lease iPhones for “low monthly payments” are one example of such scams.

Scammers consistently target fans of flagship smartphones. Example of a fake page impersonating Apple

The streaming platform discount trap

Black Friday has become a major subscriber acquisition window for subscription-based streaming services rather than a peripheral promotional event. Antenna estimates that Black Friday drove 8.9 million incremental premium subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) sign-ups in 2025 and accounted for roughly 25% of all November sign-ups, an 800,000 increase compared to 2024, when Black Friday promotions generated 8.1 million sign-ups.

This concentration of promotional activity also expands the space for abuse. As subscription platforms compete for user attention with discounts, limited-time offers, and account-based promotions, threat actors can easily repurpose the same themes across phishing pages and fraudulent payment forms. In this context, brands tied to subscriptions, billing, account access, and merchant services are used as lures: they are widely recognized, naturally associated with recurring payments and promotional offers and therefore likely to prompt user engagement.

Netflix remained among the top five online-store and subscription-service brands most frequently abused by scammers, highlighting the persistent use of streaming services as lures in brand-abuse campaigns. While the majority of observed schemes affecting this platform simply sought to phish users’ credentials, we also saw “generous offers” trying to lure users with discounts. In one example, the attackers embedded the Netflix name in a bundle with other services, such as telecom or entertainment packages. The fraudulent page is designed to collect a range of personal data. Afterwards, the attackers contact the victim via WhatsApp to ask for further information or money. Another scheme imitates the platform itself, offering fake discounted subscription deals. In both scenarios, attackers exploit trust in a globally recognized entertainment brand to increase engagement and push users toward sharing sensitive details or paying money.

Scammers create Netflix-themed fake pages to harvest personal and payment data or sell nonexistent subscriptions

Subscription entertainment brands, such as Spotify and YouTube Premium, are also being used as phishing lures to collect either payment card data through fake subscription forms or account credentials through counterfeit login pages. Informal “support” channels, such as WhatsApp chats, add credibility and help attackers guide victims in real time.

Subscription-service scams impersonate Spotify and YouTube Premium to steal payment details and account credentials

Inside the Black Friday spam wave targeting shoppers

In 2026, Black Friday–related scams continued to spread across multiple channels, with fraudulent email campaigns remaining one of the ways they reached their victims. As retailers stepped up their seasonal marketing, cybercriminals took advantage of the flood of promotional messages by sending look-alike emails. During the first two weeks of November, Kaspersky detected 220,071 spam messages related to the sales season – 50,18% more than in 2025. Over the same period, 1,728 of the identified spam messages referenced Singles’ Day promotions in Asia.

Scam campaigns built around Apple products begin long before Black Friday: fraudulent activity traditionally spikes on the eve of Apple’s keynotes and then flows seamlessly into the November sales season. In one example, a link from a spam email leads to a fake store impersonating a telecom operator, which offers the new iPhone 18 Pro Max at a tiny fraction of its retail price as a “time-limited special offer”.

An example of a detected spam email impersonating a Telenor marketing proposal. The email offers a new smartphone model for sale

The page mimics the real provider’s product page and is most likely designed to trick the user into entering payment card details.

Scammers created a fake page impersonating the Telenor online store. The users land on the website through a link in a spam email

Alongside fake stores, gamified giveaways are still a persistent email scam format of the sales season: instead of simply offering a discount, fraudsters invite users to “win” a prize, which makes users lower their guard and adds an element of excitement. Pages of this kind typically impersonate well-known retail brands and use personalized greetings, limited attempts, and guaranteed “wins” to create an impression of an exclusive, harmless lottery. The prize, of course, is predetermined and serves only as a pretext to request personal and payment card details, allegedly to cover delivery. Exploiting trust in household retail names, such schemes leave victims with compromised card data or stolen money instead of a gift.

Fake REWE-branded Black Friday giveaway offering a free gift for guessing a “secret number”

Wasted: GTA VI “offers” and other lures targeting the gaming community this November

In November 2026, the gaming industry is set for one of its most anticipated launches in years: GTA VI. Highly awaited game releases have long created openings for cybercriminal activity. In our 2024 Kaspersky Security Bulletin, we predicted that cybercriminals would seek to exploit GTA VI’s popularity. In fact, the risk is also amplified by timing: the game’s November 19 launch coincides with the seasonal sales campaigns, when users are already primed to look for discounts, bundles, and limited-time offers. This means users need to be extra cautious.

Malware campaigns typically cluster around the game itself, using the surrounding attention to disguise malicious files as related content; between June and November 2026, Kaspersky detected 27,416 malware and potentially unwanted application attacks posing as GTA VI–related content. At the same time, phishing schemes follow a separate logic: they exploit purchase intent and urgency around offers, driving users to fake pages.

In the example below, a fake store offers Brazilian users a chance to buy a PS5 subscription bundle with GTA VI included. Scammers offer payment options via a banking card or Pix. If the user pays, they never see either PlayStation or the game.

Besides GTA VI, all traditional gaming phishing and scam schemes are also present. The screenshot below shows a fraudulent website mimicking Steam that allegedly gives away $50 gift cards as part of a “Winter Gift Marathon”. To get the card, users are urged to log in to their Steam accounts, compromising their credentials.

Another scheme invites users to a Discord group chat. However, when the victim tries to enter the chat, a pop-up window appears telling them that they need to install a security module. If they click the “Install” button, a suspicious file is downloaded to their device.

From self-care to scam: how attackers target beauty and wellness fans

In addition to shopping-related scams, cybercriminals have continued to exploit consumer interest in personal health, wellness, and beauty in 2026. These themes have long been present in spam and phishing activity, as they combine broad consumer appeal with topics that often involve sensitive personal decisions and data. The continued expansion of online health services, consultations, and wellness products also makes such lures appear more familiar and plausible to users.

Weight loss was one of the health-related themes observed in spam campaigns. In one identified example, a link in a spam email redirected the recipient to a page promoting a telehealth weight-loss service. The page used likely fabricated credibility markers – such as claims of “1,000s of patients” and “600+ doctors” – to make the site appear as an established medical provider. The prompt to “qualify in 5 minutes” through an online assessment acted as the first step in the conversion funnel. Depending on the scheme, such websites may further prompt users to enter their personal and medical data into a fraudulent form, may steal money, or just sell dubious products or services under the guise of a magic pill.

An example of a weight-loss telehealth page

Another spam email targeted users concerned about skin aging. It used a health-advisory style banner and a clickbait headline presenting “The 1 Vitamin You Need if You Have Wrinkled Skin” as a dermatologist’s recommendation. By combining appeals to medical authority and social proof, such as mentioning thousands who already use this vitamin, and framing the offer as free advice through the call to action “Tap For Recipe,” the campaign lowered users’ guard.

Brand recognition in this scenario works against users: the more familiar an interface looks, the less likely a visitor is to question its authenticity. This logic forms the basis of a whole cluster of phishing campaigns that abuse the names of major tech platforms. Fraudulent pages copying login pages of these platforms reproduce the original layout, branding, and even alternative sign-in options, leaving credential entry forms as the only interactive element – everything typed into these forms goes straight to the attackers. Scammers often create pages that replicate the fonts and visual style of the original site. This example mimics an Amazon page

A common technique for stealing login credentials. Example of a fake website impersonating Shopify

A related but noisier approach relies on manufactured urgency: we detected pages masquerading as Apple support that bombard the visitor with alarming pop-ups about a suspicious Apple Pay “pre-authorization” and urge them to immediately call a “support number”. Example of a scam page exploiting a sense of urgency

Scammers consistently target fans of flagship smartphones. Example of a fake page impersonating Apple

Scammers created a fake page impersonating the Telenor online store. The users land on the website through a link in a spam email

Fake REWE-branded Black Friday giveaway offering a free gift for guessing a “secret number”

item.title: How to protect against preinstalled Android malware
item.description:
Introduction

Preinstalled malware on mobile devices is a major threat to user security and privacy. When we buy a new smartphone or tablet, we expect it to be ready to use and secure right out of the box. In some cases, however, devices ship with malware already on them. Such malware can do almost anything: display ads, collect personal data and credentials, track user activity, and more. Preinstalled malware can also turn the infected device into a tool for fraud, such as stealing credit card numbers or other sensitive information, causing financial loss and reputational damage.

We’ve previously reported cases where users bought smartphones on marketplaces with malware already preinstalled. Over the past few months, however, several large organizations have encountered malware embedded in the firmware of mobile devices. The specific risks to corporate security depend on how the devices are used and on the company’s line of business. But because the Trojan sits in the device firmware, any app can be compromised, and the potential damage is hard to overstate. This post looks at the current landscape of preinstalled threats on mobile devices, the risks they pose to corporate users, and available countermeasures, including Kaspersky solutions.

Landscape of preinstalled threats

The total number of devices with malicious code found in their firmware or system apps keeps growing. According to Kaspersky Security Network, the number of such devices detected each month has increased more than 2.5-fold over the past year.

Monthly number of Android devices with preinstalled malware detected by Kaspersky solutions, November 2025 — October 2026 (download)

Several malware families are known to spread through firmware and system apps, the most common being Keenadu and Triada. According to our data, one or another of these two families was found on 88% of infected devices in the first ten months of 2026.

The Triada backdoor (Backdoor.AndroidOS.Triada) was discovered ten years ago and has remained popular with attackers ever since. Early versions of the malware actively exploited Android vulnerabilities to gain root access and the privileges they needed. At that time, Triada was often distributed as a regular app. Over time, however, Android introduced tighter restrictions, and attackers now mostly use the preinstalled version of this backdoor. Throughout 2026, users encountered about twenty markedly distinct variants. The most common ones were Backdoor.AndroidOS.Triada.ag and Backdoor.AndroidOS.Triada.z. The latest Triada versions have two key distinguishing features: the ability to inject malicious functionality into any app on the device, system or user-installed, and a modular architecture that lets attackers tailor the malware to their current targets with additional payloads. Known modules can steal credentials for messaging and social media apps, intercept calls and text messages, replace links in browsers, siphon off cryptocurrency, and run a reverse proxy on the infected device. It’s worth stressing that by loading additional modules, attackers get virtually unlimited capabilities.

Keenadu is another preinstalled backdoor we discovered, which appeared relatively recently. The earliest known firmware version that contains this malware dates back to 2023. Even so, the number of devices infected with Keenadu is considerable: according to our data, more than 220,000 devices were infected in the first ten months of 2026.

Keenadu is similar to Triada in many ways, especially in its main architectural feature: once it’s on a device, attackers can download additional modules with any functionality and inject them into target apps. In most known Keenadu attacks, the malware was used for ad fraud, in particular to generate fake clicks. Technically, however, it can perform any action on the infected device. Notably, on first contact with the C2 servers, the backdoor versions we analyzed received a command to activate after about two and a half months. Until then, the malware showed no activity. This is probably meant to give the device owner time to install all the apps they need and settle into daily use, and to make the compromise harder to detect.

Other families of preinstalled malware exist, although they’re less common than Triada and Keenadu. They include Dwphon, Vo1d, and BADBOX. Their functionality is generally similar: mostly ad fraud and traffic redirection. Note that most cases involve phones and tablets, but preinstalled backdoors also threaten other types of devices. For example, Dwphon has turned up in the firmware of children’s smartwatches, and Vo1d samples in TV box firmware.

Corporate environment

We first saw an organization, rather than a home user, encounter preinstalled malware several years ago. That case involved the Dwphon malware. Over the past year, however, we’ve received more and more reports from different customers. In less than a year, several large organizations have come to us with the same request. After installing Kaspersky Endpoint Security for Android on brand-new, out-of-the-box devices, they saw detections of Keenadu or Triada and asked us to confirm that those detections were genuine.

Note that when we talk about corporate threats, we mean the Corporate Owned, Business Only (COBO) and Corporate Owned, Personally Enabled (COPE) usage scenarios, where the employee’s device belongs to the organization. The difference between these models is that COBO doesn’t allow personal use of the device (and usually blocks it at the software level). With COPE, the organization controls global settings but allows free personal use and, in some cases, even installation of third-party apps. By corporate environment, we mean primarily the setup with centralized procurement, where an organization buys all the devices it needs (hundreds, thousands, or even tens of thousands) for uniform use. This post doesn’t cover infections under the Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) model, where employees use infected personal devices they bought themselves to access company resources or for work communications.

Preinstalled malware appears on a new device as a result of a supply chain attack. Devices can be manufactured and flashed in different places. Likewise, different parties in the production process can create the firmware and prepare it for the device. Malicious code typically gets onto a device in one of three ways:

  1. The manufacturer installs the malware deliberately: the attackers control the entire production process and either sell infected devices cheaply under an obscure brand name or, conversely, pose as a well-known manufacturer, damaging that company’s reputation.
  2. A legitimate brand that makes the final device receives malicious firmware from a contractor acting in bad faith.
  3. A legitimate manufacturer builds the firmware in-house, but the build relies on an already infected base or code component. Here, no one directly involved in manufacturing knows the production chain has been compromised.

What risks do corporate customers face when they buy such devices? Based on the technical capabilities of preinstalled malware, we can identify the following main risks:

  • Degraded performance of infected devices: shorter battery life, overheating, and glitches in various apps. Some devices have even been known to play random sounds on their own.
  • Ads on devices, both visible to the user and hidden. They consume extra traffic and also connect the device to various websites, which creates a separate group of risks.
  • Account takeover in messaging apps, social media, and corporate resources: theft of credentials can damage the company’s reputation and lead to financial losses or even new attacks.
  • Direct financial losses, such as cryptocurrency theft.
  • Theft of confidential data and secrets: in effect, spying on corporate devices.
  • Use in a proxy botnet: the organization’s infected devices can relay arbitrary traffic to any internet resources.
  • Use in a DDoS botnet: infected devices can be enlisted to launch DDoS attacks on any target. Reputational risks come into play here as well.
  • External access to the corporate infrastructure through a proxy module. Infected devices are known to have been used as residential proxies to infect other devices on the same local network.
  • Device downtime: attackers who disable corporate devices in active use can disrupt operations.

Note that not all of the attack scenarios involving preinstalled malware listed above have been seen in real-world incidents. However, Triada and BADBOX, for example, have already expanded their functionality: besides displaying ads, they now steal accounts. We can therefore expect preinstalled malware to keep gaining capabilities that pose even higher risks.

Using Kaspersky solutions to mitigate risks

Mobile Device Management (MDM) is a separate category of solutions built to manage mobile devices, and it helps mitigate infection risks in corporate environments. With MDM, IT teams can centrally configure smartphones, tablets and laptops, enforce security policies, and control app installation. This significantly reduces the risk of infection caused by user actions, because it prevents a user from installing an APK from an attacker’s message, a malicious website, or a rogue app store listing.

However, these measures alone are not effective against preinstalled Trojans. Centralized mobile device management alone is not enough to contain threats like Triada and Keenadu. It must be complemented by protection that can detect malware, including any already present on a device before the company starts using it. The best approach is to combine management and protection in a single agent with a unified console, which simplifies rollout and day-to-day operation: IT teams only need to deploy and maintain one application instead of two.

Kaspersky Next product line, starting with Kaspersky Next EDR Optimum, combines Advanced MDM functionality with antivirus protection. The antivirus engine scans files and installed apps and provides real-time protection. Kaspersky Next can detect malware on Android devices, even in preinstalled apps, and alert administrators to any threats it finds. This allows spotting an infection on a device that nominally complies with corporate policies.

Triada detection report in the unified KSC console (screenshot in Russian)

Note that it’s technically impossible for either antivirus tools or the OS itself to remove preinstalled malware from the system partition. However, Kaspersky Next lowers the risk of buying a whole batch of devices and then finding a preinstalled Trojan that is hard or impossible to remove by reflashing. If Kaspersky Next detects malware like Triada or Keenadu, it alerts the IT administrator, who can then contain the threat by blocking the device’s internet access, clearing app data, rotating passwords, or locking the device entirely. Administrators can monitor and manage the infected device from the unified console of the Kaspersky Security Center.

Threat monitoring in the unified KSC console

Companies planning a mobile infrastructure should account for the risk of encountering preinstalled malware. Before ordering a large batch of devices, we recommend inspecting and pilot-testing sample units. We should stress that this measure is no substitute for installing security software on every device used in the organization. Even if the tests come out fine, an unscrupulous supplier may have deliberately sent clean units for inspection. Protection must also be continuous because, for example, the device update system could come under attack.

Manufacturers need to check devices and firmware code for malware just as customers do. Whether the firmware is written in-house or by a contractor, the result can contain malicious code, as we noted earlier. To detect preinstalled threats, you need a file scanning solution that can respond quickly when it finds malware. Kaspersky Scan Engine is one of the Kaspersky products designed for this task. The engine uses the latest detection technologies to identify a wide range of cyberthreats, including preinstalled ones. It integrates easily into a variety of workflows. For example, it can connect to a software build pipeline or any other system that needs to check files for malicious code.

Triada detection in Kaspersky Scan Engine

If Kaspersky Next detects malware like Triada or Keenadu, it alerts the IT administrator, who can then contain the threat by blocking the device’s internet access, clearing app data, rotating passwords, or locking the device entirely. Administrators can monitor and manage the infected device from the unified console of the Kaspersky Security Center.

Companies planning a mobile infrastructure should account for the risk of encountering preinstalled malware. Before ordering a large batch of devices, we recommend inspecting and pilot-testing sample units. We should stress that this measure is no substitute for installing security software on every device used in the organization. Even if the tests come out fine, an unscrupulous supplier may have deliberately sent clean units for inspection. Protection must also be continuous because, for example, the device update system could come under attack.

Manufacturers need to check devices and firmware code for malware just as customers do. Whether the firmware is written in-house or by a contractor, the result can contain malicious code, as we noted earlier. To detect preinstalled threats, you need a file scanning solution that can respond quickly when it finds malware. Kaspersky Scan Engine is one of the Kaspersky products designed for this task. The engine uses the latest detection technologies to identify a wide range of cyberthreats, including preinstalled ones. It integrates easily into a variety of workflows. For example, it can connect to a software build pipeline or any other system that needs to check files for malicious code.
